title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 deterministic intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal (requested model: gpt-5-mini) produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared proposal examined by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. The archived analysis used the exact McNemar two-sided convention implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01); this yields two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed single discordant pair. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the marginal numeric verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though one archived discordant episode shows the loop corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as translating operator intent into device configurations, planning multi-step changes, and proposing repairs. Recent system reports and surveys emphasize that production safety and reliability hinge on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A widely proposed operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and repairs are applied when violations appear. Despite conceptual agreement, controlled measurements isolating the verifier’s marginal contribution under fixed-model proposals are rare. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer the narrow operational question: given identical initial model proposals (shared-initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone?
sections.related_work: Deterministic verification tooling and formal analyses for network configurations (header-space analysis and route-model verifiers) can check reachability, isolation, and update-safety and are foundational to NetOps verification [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems instantiate LLM-based intent translators and emphasize the need for validators and guardrails to reach operational reliability (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and other agentic NetOps proposals) [INTA, 2025; Confucius, 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns appear across structured-generation domains as a practical route to reduce incorrect outputs; analogous ideas appear in domain-specific constrained-generation systems [PoeTone; INTA]. Failure-mode studies of LLM-driven automation document hallucination, overconfidence, and tool-integration errors, motivating verifier-in-the-loop architectures and human oversight [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. Prior work, however, seldom provides preregistered, artifact-backed ablations that isolate verifier effect sizes while holding initial proposals fixed; this study contributes one such measurement and clarifies its conditional scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: We preregistered the confirmatory study (study_id: cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) that fixed the research question, task-generation seeds, inclusion/exclusion rules, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before execution. The primary confirmatory hypothesis: pairing an LLM with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduces verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM proposal alone (paired within-task). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task corpus and strata: A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated with the archived deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using preregistered seeds. Tasks were stratified into VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), and static-route-change (166). To maintain construct validity with the chosen verifier, the task generator constrained allowed_fields to {admin, mtu, vlan}; tasks that referenced features outside the verifier’s modeled set would have been routed to an unmodeled-feature cohort and excluded (no such exclusions occurred in this run). Each task contains initial_state, expected_final_state, and an explicit required_sequence; representative task manifests are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Generation semantics and experimental control: To isolate verifier+repair marginal effect conditional on identical proposals, we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal which served both as the baseline output and as the input evaluated by the guarded arm. The guarded arm invoked a repair-stage provider call only when the deterministic validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This preregistered design avoids conflating verifier-guided regeneration with verifier+repair impact on fixed model proposals.

Models, adapter, and validator: Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); the model configuration is archived in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version: gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation). The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the validator's property set and violation-code→severity mapping are archived in the evidence bundle. The guarded arm allowed at most one automated repair iteration per preregistered contract.

Confirmatory analysis plan and exact McNemar implementation: The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implements the exact two-sided test by treating the discordant pair count n = n10 + n01 and performing an exact binomial test B(n, 0.5) on the observed count n10 (the count of pairs where guarded==1 and baseline==0). The two-sided p-value is computed as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} with X ~ Binomial(n, 0.5), truncated at 1.0; this computation rule and rationale are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference were computed with B = 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), resampling whole paired observations with replacement while preserving pairing. Missingness and retries: the preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automatic retries for transient provider errors; the run followed the stopping rule (complete N = 500 pairs) and logged all provider-call metadata.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcomes: The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500, model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500, repair-stage calls = 1), and failed_episode_count = 0. Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar and bootstrap CI: Using the archived exact-binomial convention on discordant pairs (n = 1, n10 = 1, n01 = 0), the two-sided exact McNemar p-value computed by the analysis executor is p = 1.00 (p_two-sided = 2 × min{0.5, 0.5} = 1.0). The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729); bootstrap details and code references are archived with analysis artifacts.

Repair activity and discordant-pair provenance: Observed repair-stage calls = 1 across the entire run; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1), i.e., the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The full per-task records (prompts, raw LLM outputs, validator diagnostics including violation codes and severity, and repair prompt/response traces) are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256 recorded in the execution manifest). The discordant episode is deterministically locatable by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for pairs where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because exactly one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set this filter returns the single episode and its repair-stage provider-call trace. The archived per-task validator diagnostics include the exact violation code(s) and the repair prompt/response used; these records provide the concrete evidence that a guarded repair corrected a baseline failure.

Secondary analyses: Pre-registered per-violation-class analyses were uninformative because observed violation counts were nearly zero; there were no meaningful per-class counts to support class-level inference. The preregistration assumed a baseline error prevalence around 0.30 for power planning; the observed prevalence (1/500 failures) created a ceiling effect that reduced sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric. Analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, and missingness_summary.csv) are archived and show zero exclusions and no missing pairs.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation: Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested model (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, deterministic validator modeling allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}, and a single repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and measured verifier+repair gain on the verifier pass-rate metric was small (absolute improvement 0.002). However, this outcome does not imply verifiers are unnecessary. First, the verifier produced at least one concrete correction (the single archived discordant episode), demonstrating corrective potential. Second, in workloads with higher baseline error prevalence, broader verifier coverage, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or with different generation semantics (verifier-guided regeneration) the verifier+repair contribution could be substantially larger.

Design-choice implications: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals and answer a specific operational question about marginal benefit when a single proposal is fixed. This design does not evaluate alternate operational strategies such as verifier-in-the-loop regeneration, multi-iteration repair budgets, or independent-condition generation—each targets different cost/latency tradeoffs. Practitioners should select experimental semantics matched to deployment semantics when estimating guardrail benefits.

Validity threats and interpretation cautions: Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic seed-based task generation, and automated exclusion rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity depends on the verifier’s modeled property set and severity mapping: our pass/fail outcome is defined relative to that mapping archived in the evidence bundle. External validity is limited: one requested model family and one validator on a synthetic verifier-scoped corpus do not establish cross-model or production generality. The observed ceiling effect (very low baseline error prevalence) invalidated preregistered power assumptions and reduced sensitivity for small effect detection; this is reflected in the exact McNemar p = 1.00 under the archived two-sided binomial convention for the single discordant pair. All numeric tables and analysis logs are archived for inspection.

Operational recommendations grounded in artifacts: (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence and verifier coverage on representative operational data before allocating automated-repair budget—when baseline error is already extremely low, marginal pass-rate gains for a verifier may be small for the pass-rate metric. (2) Align verifier property coverage with operator safety priorities; the archived validator-spec and violation-code mapping should be inspected to assess coverage. (3) Choose generation semantics consistent with operational goals: shared_initial_candidate minimizes model calls while verifier-guided regeneration may increase final-pass probability at higher generation cost. The repository of execution logs and exemplar repair traces supports these operational evaluations.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the supplied synthetic verifier-scoped corpus and with the requested model/validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the two-sided binomial convention implemented). The result documents a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal error prevalence is extremely low and verifier coverage is constrained, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a verifier on this metric may be negligible, though the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures (one archived corrected episode). We recommend operators measure baseline proposal error prevalence and verifier coverage on representative workloads and align generation/repair semantics with operational priorities. The evidence bundle archives every prompt, model output, validator trace, provider-call trace, and analysis artifact needed to deterministically reproduce and inspect these claims.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; the task payloads in the archive show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 must be interpreted in that context and reflects the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair_id entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
